title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
authors: Dario Bocchi, Matteo Negri, Flavio Nicoletti, Francesco D'Amico
abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.
summary: This paper applies statistical physics tools, like the replica method, to analyze the generalization limits of token prediction in LLMs. It contrasts continuous embedding learning with the more constrained regime imposed by discrete vocabularies. The work provides theoretical insights into how embedding geometry dictates the fundamental learning capacity of modern language models.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the geometric structure of token embeddings and the discrete nature of vocabulary affect the generalization capabilities of large language models (LLMs) when viewed as a classification problem.
main_result: The analysis establishes distinct theoretical thresholds and learning dynamics for continuous versus discrete (vocabulary) embeddings, showing that the optimal learner prioritizes resolving directions with high variance in the vocabulary space.
method: The study employs advanced techniques from statistical physics, notably the replica method and saddle-point calculations, to derive the generalization error and storage capacity in the thermodynamic limit.
model_or_system: The core model is the 'token perceptron,' a minimal solvable teacher-student learning system. It compares continuous inputs (like spherical embeddings) to discrete inputs drawn from a finite vocabulary $Z$.
key_observables: Generalization error ($\epsilon_g$), storage capacity ($\alpha_c$), and the student-teacher overlap ($r$).
important_parameters: Embedding dimension ($d$), vocabulary size ($D$), dataset load ($\alpha = P/N$), and the replica symmetry breaking parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the replica method, the replica symmetric (RS) ansatz, and approximations like the large-$d$ limit for tractability.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares the learning process for continuous embeddings (on $S^{d-1}$) versus discrete vocabulary embeddings (using Voronoi cell identification).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the continuous embedding case, deriving the exact recovery threshold. It then transitions to the vocabulary case, analyzing the constraints imposed by the discrete embedding geometry using spectral closure techniques.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the use of replica methods and capacity calculations mirrors techniques used in spin-glass models and disordered systems, providing a theoretical framework for understanding pattern retrieval in complex, geometrically constrained systems.
